source_name.short_meaning: The Supreme, meaning that which transcends all limitations and imperfections of matter: in short, the Transcendental Reality
source_name.commentary:
The Supreme, meaning that which transcends all limitations and imperfections of matter: in short, the Transcendental Reality. The Spirit is other than matter, and that in its presence, the vestures of matter, borrowing their dynamism from Him, play their parts rhythmically at all times. This has been the assertion found chorusly repeated in all the Upaniṣads and in the entire Vedantic literature. Śaṅkara in ātma Bodha points out that the Self is other than the three bodies and that He functions in the microcosm as a king in the nation. It was also said therein that matter borrows its energy from the Spirit and continues its activity "as the world from the Sun". Kaṭhopaniṣad and the Gītā guide us from the outer levels of our personality, stage by stage, into the inner-most sanctum, and there, the teachers declare, is He the Infinite, transcending all, reigning in His own glory. "In short, that which remains other than the cause and effect-māyā and matter-is He, the Parama ātman. In Viṣṇu Purāṇa this Supreme is glorified as Maha Viṣṇu (paramātmā)"—Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.4.10.

Dehendriya-mano-buddhi-prakṛtibhyo vilakṣaṇam.

Tat-vṛtti-sākṣiṇam vidyād ātmānaṃ rājavat sadā.

As the world from the Sun (sūryālokamayā janāḥ). — Ātma Bodha 20.

इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः । मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः ॥ — Gītā 3.42.

परमात्मा च सर्वेषामाधारः परमेश्वरः । विष्णुर्नाम सर्ववेदेषु वेदान्तेषु च गीयते ॥ — Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.4.10.
